# Preface {.unnumbered}

Your phone records your voice, compresses it, sends it as radio waves and
rebuilds it on the other side. Your music player turns lists of numbers into
sound. A Wi-Fi card squeezes hundreds of megabits per second through a noisy
channel. All of this is **digital signal processing** (DSP): the art of
manipulating signals that have been turned into numbers.

## Who this book is for

This book is written for computer science and engineering students in the last
years of their degree. You are expected to program comfortably and to remember
basic algebra and a little calculus. You are **not** expected to know complex
analysis, Fourier series or transforms: every mathematical tool is introduced
from scratch, when it is needed and only as far as it is needed.

## How this book works

Every idea comes with code you can run. Figures are not drawn by hand: they are
produced by the Python code next to them every time the book is built, so what
you read is what the code really does.

You can work with the code in three ways, from least to most effort:

1. **Read it.** Code and results appear together in the HTML and PDF editions.
2. **Try it in the browser.** Boxes marked *Try it* in the HTML edition contain
   editable code that runs in your browser. Change a parameter, press *Run*,
   and see what happens. Nothing to install.
3. **Run everything locally.** One container image holds Python, the libraries
   and the tools that build this book. @sec-running-the-code shows how to open
   it as a JupyterLab session or a VS Code dev container. You only need Docker.

## How to read it

Part I treats signals as lists of numbers and as vectors. Part II introduces
frequency, the central idea of the book. Part III shows how to change signals
with filters. Part IV connects the digital world with the analog one. Part V
puts everything together in a software modem that sends bits through a
simulated telephone line.

The chapters are meant to be read in order. Mathematical refreshers live in
@sec-math-toolbox, so you can look things up without breaking the flow.

## Acknowledgements

The overall approach, signals first, frequency as a change of basis and a
communication system as the final project, is inspired by
*Signal Processing for Communications* [@prandoni2008]. This book is an
independent text with its own explanations, examples and code.
